bib.title: Software Engineering for Machine Learning: A Case Study

question: How do Microsoft software teams integrate machine learning into their engineering processes, what challenges and best practices result, and how mature are their ML practices?
hypothesis: Respondents' perceived challenges vary with their amount of AI experience.
contributions: A description of how several Microsoft software engineering teams work cast into a nine-stage workflow for integrating machine learning
A set of best practices for building applications and platforms relying on machine learning
A custom machine-learning process maturity model for assessing the progress of software teams
A discussion of three fundamental differences in how software engineering applies to ML-centric components vs. previous application domains

method.summary: Two-phase qualitative and survey study at Microsoft: 14 semi-structured interviews chosen by snowball sampling, then an open-ended questionnaire sent to 4195 mailing-list members (551 responses). Open responses were card sorted; challenge frequencies were compared across AI-experience tertiles with logistic regression; a six-statement Activity Maturity Index was validated against self-rated effectiveness.
method.task: Empirical case study of ML software engineering practice (interviews and survey)

datasets.name: Interviews
datasets.size: 14 software engineers, largely senior leadership (Table I: I1-I14)
datasets.source: Microsoft; snowball sampling from leaders of mature ML teams (e.g. Bing), AI-centric teams (e.g. Cortana), and company-wide AI/ML trainers
datasets.preprocessing: semi-structured, specialised to each informant's role

datasets.name: Survey
datasets.split: Experience buckets low/medium/high by 33rd and 67th percentile of years of AI experience (N=308 for Table II)
datasets.source: internal Microsoft mailing lists on AI and ML
datasets.preprocessing: open-response items card sorted by 2 to 4 researchers, then reviewed by whole team

inference.samples: one survey wave, 551 responses; no repeats

parameters.experience_buckets: low/medium/high, 33rd and 67th percentile of personal years of AI experience
parameters.respondent_mix: Data and applied science 42%, Software engineering 32%, Program management 17%, Research 7%, other 1%; 21% managers, 79% individual contributors

metrics.name: Activity Maturity Index (AMI)
metrics.definition: Average of Likert agreement (1-5) with six statements S1..S6 (goals defined, consistent, documented, automated, measured and tracked, continuously improved) for each workflow stage a respondent spent most time on

metrics.name: Activity Effectiveness (AE)
metrics.definition: 'How effective do you think your team's practices around this activity are on a scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent)?'

metrics.name: Overall Effectiveness (OE)
metrics.definition: 'How effectively does your team work with AI on a scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent)'

eval.protocol: Spearman correlation of AMI with AE; logistic regression of challenge frequency controlling for personal AI experience, team AI experience, overall work experience, concurrent AI projects, formal ML education; ANOVA and Scott-Knott test on OE across nine application domains. Self-reported data, no objective baseline.

prompts.text: S1: My team has goals defined for what to accomplish with this activity. S2: My team does this activity in a consistent manner. S3: My team has largely documented the practices related to this activity. S4: My team does this activity mostly in an automated way. S5: My team measures and tracks how effective we are at completing this activity. S6: My team continuously improves our practices related to this activity.

results.claim: The maturity model is descriptive over six dimensions (defined goals, consistent, documented, automated, measured and tracked, continuously improved); maturity levels like CMM are not defined.

Authors identify three fundamental differences: data management is harder than code management, model customization and reuse need ML skills, and models are entangled so non-monotonic error propagation occurs.
results.setup: Discussion, Section VII, from interviews and survey

limits: Case study at one large company (Microsoft); some findings may be specific to those teams.
Interviews and survey are self-selected and self-reported; findings are informants' perceptions.
The maturity model is a first attempt, triangulated against equally subjective measures with no objective baseline; maturity levels not defined.
Response rate was 13.6%; 308 of 551 respondents entered the experience-bucket analysis (Table II N=308).
Best practices are reported respondent opinions, not tested; no effect sizes for any practice.
2019 study of pre-LLM ML; no LLM or prompt workflows.
practices: Build a rock-solid automated data pipeline that loads and massages data so engineers can try many algorithm and hyper-parameter permutations (V.A).
Integrate ML development support into traditional software infrastructure covering all nine stages (V.A).
Reuse data as much as possible to reduce duplicated effort; make datasets available subject to compliance (V.B).
Blend data management tools with ML frameworks to avoid fragmenting data and model management (V.B).
Version data rigorously; tag each model with a provenance tag and each dataset with its origin and extraction code version (V.B).
Scaffold engineer education with internal conferences, weekly forums and mailing lists (V.C).
Use interpretable models or visualization for debugging, and modularise multi-model systems in layered architectures (V.D).
Evaluate with combo-flighting, multi-metric score cards and human evaluation for sensitive categories; keep a human in the loop on errors (V.E).
Automate training and deployment, use common versioning repositories for ML and non-ML code, and couple ML and non-ML sprints and standups (V.E).
Use data sheets and data diff tools to document and compare datasets (VII.A).
